title: What must Portuguese organizations tell and train staff about whistleblowing under Law 93/2021?
description: Portugal's Law 93/2021 internal reporting channels: who needs one, the 7 day and 3 month deadlines, fines, and what staff and channel handlers should learn.
shortAnswer: Portugal's Law 93/2021, the general whistleblower protection regime, requires legal persons with 50 or more workers, and financial sector entities of any size, to run internal reporting channels open to all workers. Reports must be acknowledged within seven days and answered within three months. The law sets no general training duty for companies, but its confidentiality rules, anti-retaliation presumptions, and fines mean channel handlers, managers, and every worker need to understand how the channel works.
keyTakeaways: Article 8 of Law 93/2021 requires internal channels in legal persons with 50 or more workers and, regardless of size, entities covered by the Directive's financial services and related acts.
Obliged entities must acknowledge a report within seven days and tell the reporter what follow up was taken within three months (Article 11).
Confidentiality extends to anyone who receives information about a report, even if not responsible for handling it (Article 18(2)), which makes it a whole workforce training point.
Adverse acts within two years of a report are presumed retaliatory (Article 21(6)); breaching confidentiality or retaliating is a very serious offense with fines up to EUR 250,000 for legal persons.
MENAC, the national anticorruption mechanism, enforces the regime and recommends at least two designated channel operators, one with legal training.
regulator: Mecanismo Nacional Anticorrupção (MENAC), with sector authorities where special EU regimes apply
appliesTo: Private and public legal persons employing 50 or more workers
Entities within Parts I.B and II of the Annex to Directive (EU) 2019/1937 (financial services, AML, transport safety, environment), regardless of size
Portuguese branches of legal persons based abroad
Municipalities with 10,000 or more inhabitants and 50 or more workers
Managers, channel operators, and all workers, contractors, volunteers, and trainees who may report or receive reports

sections.heading: What is Law 93/2021 and who must have an internal reporting channel?

blocks.text: [Law 93/2021](https://files.diariodarepublica.pt/1s/2021/12/24400/0000300015.pdf) of December 20, 2021 (Lei n.º 93/2021, regime geral de proteção de denunciantes de infrações, often shortened to RGPDI) transposes the [EU Whistleblower Directive](/regulations/eu-whistleblower-directive-obligations), Directive (EU) 2019/1937. Under Article 31 it entered into force 180 days after publication, in June 2022.

Article 8(1) requires internal reporting channels in legal persons, including the State and other public law entities, that employ 50 or more workers, and, regardless of headcount, in entities within the scope of the EU acts in Parts I.B and II of the Directive's Annex, which brings most [financial services](/industries/financial-services) firms into scope. Article 8(2) allows private obliged entities with 50 to 249 workers to share resources for receiving and following up reports. Article 8(3) extends the duty to Portuguese branches of legal persons based abroad. Article 8(6) exempts municipalities with fewer than 10,000 inhabitants.

Protection is wide. Under Article 5, a reporter can be a worker in the private, social, or public sector, a service provider, contractor or supplier, a shareholder or board member including non-executives, or a volunteer or trainee, paid or unpaid. It also covers information obtained in a relationship that has ended or during recruitment.

sections.heading: What must the internal channel do?

blocks.text: The channel must allow secure submission and follow up of reports and keep the reporter's identity confidential or anonymous. The core requirements are in Articles 9 to 11 and 20.

items: Article 9(1): guarantee completeness, integrity, and retention of reports, confidentiality of the reporter and of third parties named, and prevent access by unauthorized persons.

Article 9(2) to (4): channels are operated internally by designated persons or services; only receipt may be outsourced; independence, impartiality, confidentiality, data protection, secrecy, and absence of conflicts must be guaranteed.

Article 10(1) and (2): workers must be able to report in writing and or orally, anonymously or named; where oral reports are allowed, by phone or voice message and, on request, in a face to face meeting.
Article 11(1): acknowledge receipt within seven days and inform the reporter, clearly and accessibly, of the requirements and competent authorities for external reporting.
Article 11(3): communicate the measures planned or taken and their grounds within three months of receipt; Article 11(4): on request, communicate the outcome within 15 days of conclusion.
Article 20(1): keep a register of reports and retain them for at least five years, and longer while related court or administrative proceedings are pending.

blocks.text: Article 7(2) explains why the internal channel matters. A reporter may go straight to an external authority only in listed cases, for example where no internal channel exists, where there is a risk of retaliation, where the internal channel did not respond within the Article 11 deadlines, or where the matter is a crime or an offense punishable by a fine over EUR 50,000. A channel that staff do not know about or trust gives up that first opportunity to deal with the issue.

Not for private obliged entities in so many words. The only express training duty is in Article 13(3), which requires competent authorities to give the officials who handle external reports specific training. Failing to do so is a serious offense under Article 27(3)(l).

Training inside companies follows from three other rules. First, Article 18(2) extends the confidentiality duty to anyone who has received information about a report, even if they are not responsible for handling it, so a line manager who hears about a report in a corridor is bound. Second, Article 21(6) presumes that adverse acts taken within two years of a report, such as changes to duties, negative appraisals, non renewal of a fixed-term contract, or dismissal, were retaliation unless proven otherwise. Third, Article 10(1) and Article 27(3)(d) require the channel to be available to all workers, which is hard to demonstrate if workers have not been told it exists.

blocks.title: Where a training duty does apply
blocks.text: Entities covered by Portugal's general anti-corruption regime (RGPC) must also run a training program and a whistleblowing channel under that regime. See [Portugal's anti-corruption regime training](/regulations/portugal-anti-corruption-regime-training).

sections.heading: What does MENAC guidance expect from the channel and its operators?

blocks.text: The Mecanismo Nacional Anticorrupção (MENAC) processes offenses and applies fines under Article 29(1), except where a sector authority is competent. Its [synthesis note on the internal reporting channel](https://menac.pt/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/canal-de-denuncia-interna-sintese.pdf) (Canal de Denúncia Interna: cuidados metodológicos e normativos de dinamização) sets out practical expectations that translate directly into communication and training tasks.

items: The channel should be available internally, for example on the intranet, to all managers, workers, trainees, and volunteers, whatever the type of contract or pay.
At least two people should be designated to receive, analyze, and follow up reports, to manage conflicts of interest.
Operators should ideally come from different departments and backgrounds, with at least one having legal training; designating people of both sexes may also be appropriate.
Receipt must be confirmed within seven days and, where feasible, the reporter informed of the effects of the report within three months.
The reporting form can prompt for what happened, when, who was involved, where, how the reporter knows, who else knows, and where evidence can be found.

blocks.text: Managers in particular need case based practice, because the presumption in Article 21(6) shifts the burden of proof to the organization. A broader method is in [whistleblower policy training requirements](/regulations/whistleblower-policy-training-requirements) and [how to design a compliance training program](/guides/how-to-design-a-compliance-training-program).

sections.heading: What are the penalties under Law 93/2021?

blocks.text: Article 27 sets two tiers of administrative offenses. Very serious offenses carry fines of EUR 1,000 to 25,000 for individuals and EUR 10,000 to 250,000 for legal persons; serious offenses carry EUR 500 to 12,500 and EUR 1,000 to 125,000 respectively. Attempt and negligence are punishable, with maximums halved.

items: Very serious (Article 27(1)): preventing a report or its follow up, retaliation, breaching confidentiality, and knowingly reporting false information.

Serious (Article 27(3)): having no internal channel; a channel without the Article 9(1) guarantees; handling in breach of independence or conflict rules; a channel not open to all workers or not allowing anonymous, written, or oral reports; missing the 7 day acknowledgment; failing to retain reports for five years; recording oral reports without consent.

blocks.text: Under Article 21(4), anyone who retaliates must also compensate the reporter. Article 26(2) makes contract clauses that limit reporting void, which is worth stating in manager training because confidentiality clauses in settlement agreements are a common risk.

sections.heading: Has Law 93/2021 changed since it was adopted?

blocks.text: As at November 2026, the European Commission's national transposition database for Directive 2019/1937 lists Law 93/2021 and Law 69/2025 of December 22, 2025, which implements the EU crypto-assets regulation and amends the Directive's annex at EU level. Organizations in the crypto-asset sector should check how Law 69/2025 affects their reporting channel scope. This page reflects the text of Law 93/2021 as published.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry defines the reporting channel as a set of concepts first, such as who may report, the deadlines, confidentiality, and the retaliation presumption, then links each to the roles that need it and the assessment that proves understanding. Channel operators and managers get scenario assessment; the wider workforce gets a short, evidenced awareness module.

faqs.q: Can a Portuguese company with fewer than 50 workers ignore Law 93/2021?
faqs.a: Only if it is not within the financial services and related EU acts listed in Parts I.B and II of the Directive's Annex. Those entities need a channel regardless of size. Smaller firms outside that scope have no duty to set up a channel, but their workers can still report externally and are protected.

faqs.q: Can the internal channel be run by an outside provider?
faqs.a: Partly. Article 9(3) allows channels to be operated externally only for receiving reports. Follow up must be done by persons or services designated inside the organization, with guarantees of independence, impartiality, confidentiality, and absence of conflicts of interest under Article 9(4).

faqs.q: How long must whistleblowing reports be kept in Portugal?
faqs.a: At least five years under Article 20(1), and longer while court or administrative proceedings about the report are pending. Oral reports may be recorded or transcribed only with the reporter's consent, and the reporter can review and sign the transcript or minutes.

The Mecanismo Nacional Anticorrupção (MENAC) processes offenses and applies fines under Article 29(1). Where an entity is covered by a sector specific EU whistleblowing regime, the authority with sanctioning power under that regime is competent instead.
